content:
Apple has today released its 2027 system updates, which include a range of new Screen Time and parental control features aimed at giving parents more effective control over how their children use devices. Details below.

Today's update includes important parental control improvements

Apple today rolled out iOS 27, iPadOS 27 and macOS 27, describing the suite of tools as a "powerful new and intuitive set of tools to help parents build a safer digital experience for their kids", most of which were previewed during the WWDC26 keynote back in June.

The new features revolve around four main areas: the content children can access, who they can contact, the time they spend on their devices, and how parents manage all of the above.

All of the above fall under the protection and restrictions of a Child Account. Apple says children under the age of 13 (or the legal minimum age in their country or region) must use a Child Account, while those under 18 can opt in.

Alongside iOS 27, Apple has also simplified the process of setting up a new Child Account. Parents can choose to start with a small number of essential apps, a recommended starter bundle, or pick which Apple apps their child can use from the outset.

Once a parent finishes setting up a Child Account, they can select which apps and websites their child can use, and set age and content restrictions for movies, TV shows, music, books and other media.

Parents can now also make use of a new Ask to Browse feature – where a child can request to view a blocked website in Safari on iPhone, iPad and Mac, and the parent can then approve or deny it in Messages. This is similar to the existing Ask to Buy, which already requires parental approval before a child can download an app or make an in-app purchase.

Parents can also require their child to get approval before adding a new contact, set shared or individual daily time limits for categories such as Entertainment, Games and Social Media, and create schedules dictating which apps can be used under different circumstances. These schedules can also vary depending on the day of the week.

Screen Time itself has also been redesigned with a new architecture, which Apple says allows parental controls to sync faster between devices in a Family Sharing group. Parents can now see at a glance a weekly usage summary and their child's most-used apps, temporarily pause access to a particular device, reinstate access after a set period of time, and quickly switch between different schedules.

The Communication Safety feature has also been expanded beyond nudity detection. It can now block shared photos or videos containing blood or violence, while also displaying warnings and additional support resources.

Time limits have also become more flexible. Parents can create their own app categories, move apps between them, and assign a time limit at the same time as approving a new app via Ask to Buy. Websites associated with a particular app can also automatically follow the same time limit.

Apple says its suggested time limits are based on a child's age and research from experts. Apple is also working with the American Academy of Pediatrics to adapt its Family Media Plan into a guide for parents using Apple products.

Finally, Apple reminds that all devices in a Family Sharing group must be running version 27 software in order to take advantage of the new Screen Time experience.
